extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (metaphysics, metaphysical anthropology)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length philosophical exposition arguing for the indestructibility/immortality of our true nature (the will/Idea), contrasting species permanence with individual transience and using metaphysical, empirical, and phenomenological arguments. Targets understanding of Ideas, time, and the subjective/objective distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension of the doctrine of Ideas as criterion for philosophising
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato rightly bases the whole of philosophy upon the knowledge of the doctrine of Ideas, i.e., upon the perception of the universal in the particular; he made the comprehension of it the criterion of capacity for philosophising in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the universal (Ideas/species) in the particular is presented as the essential intellectual capacity for genuine philosophy; those who can see the universal will share the immediate conviction about the nature of things (including immortality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Touchstone of truth: comparison with the utterances of the healthy mind
rubrics_metrics.description: If the comparison of the results of a system with the utterances of the healthy mind is supposed to be a touchstone of its truth, apply this test to metaphysical systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author invokes this test to reject the Cartesian / pre-Kantian view that makes individuals utterly contingent; the 'healthy mind' intuition supports continuity/immortality claims. Use common-sense, immediate convictions as a heuristic for evaluating metaphysical theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circle as the universal symbol of nature (recurrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout and everywhere the true symbol of nature is the circle, because it is the schema or type of recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret natural recurrence—from stellar orbits to cycles of birth/death—as evidence that permanence (a nature/species) emerges through cyclical repetition; the circular schema grounds the claim that the real is preserved through recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy between sleep and death (temporal immortality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Death is for the species what sleep is for the individual: there is no radical difference between sleep and death for the persistence of the true nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the life-cycles of insects (cocoon, egg, chrysalis) and human nightly sleep as analogies showing that apparent cessation does not imply annihilation; this supports a view of temporal, recurrent continuity rather than absolute end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species permanence vs. individual transience (Ideas as true being)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato attributed true being to the Ideas alone, i.e., to the species; to the individuals only a ceaseless arising and passing away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate being by distinguishing Idea/species (enduring, real) from individual phenomena (temporal, phenomenal). The criterion for 'true being' is its permanence across temporal variations rather than momentary individuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time as a form/limitation of the intellect; thing-in-itself is timeless
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant teaches that our intellect presents the phenomenal world in time and does not comprehend the true ultimate nature of things; time is a form and limitation of our intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To assess claims about immortality, abstract from the temporal form of cognition: what appears as beginning and end in time may be mere appearances; true being belongs to the timeless thing-in-itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical regeneration implies non-annihilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations that creatures vanish and reappear (e.g., insects, infusoria) suggest that what vanishes and what appears are the same in nature, i.e., death for the individual corresponds to renewal for the species rather than absolute annihilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical examples (insect winter-sleep, eggs, observations by Burdach and Nitzsch) as supporting evidence that continual generation points to continuity of the underlying essence rather than creation ex nihilo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphysical (subjective) experiment: impossibility of conceiving world without the ego
rubrics_metrics.description: If one tries to imagine the world continuing without oneself (after one's death), the attempt fails: the ego is the immediate element in consciousness for which the world is brought about; one cannot subjectively eliminate the ego.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This imaginative test is offered as an argument for the subjective continuity of existence: the ego's inseparability from the world in consciousness supports the claim that subjective existence cannot be conceived as entirely annihilated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will to live rooted in species; distinguish individual and species motives
rubrics_metrics.description: The will to live manifests in the individual as hunger and fear of death, and in relation to the species as sexual instinct and passionate care for the offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining behavior or biological organization, evaluate whether a phenomenon serves individual survival or the perpetuation of the species (nature is stingy to individuals but prodigal toward species propagation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natura nihil facit supervacaneum — nature's parsimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature acts according to the law of parsimony (natura nihil facit supervacaneum); it gives nothing superfluous and withholds redundant endowments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use biological examples (caterpillars without eyes, minimal organs) to assess claims about design or purpose in nature; apparent insufficiencies are expressions of nature's economical allocation toward species ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immanent proof of immortality from necessary being (existence through infinite past)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because one already exists after an infinite past of changes, it is inconceivable that one could ever not be; thus what exists does so necessarily — an immanent, internal proof of imperishableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This philosophical argument claims that our present existence despite infinite past time implies necessity of existence (not contingent beginning); use it as an internal (non-empirical) justificatory criterion for immortality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of the subjective (idealistic) starting-point for philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: The right starting-point for philosophy is essentially and necessarily the subjective (idealistic); proceeding from the objective leads to materialism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the subjective/idealistic perspective (things-as-for-a-subject) when constructing metaphysical explanations; evaluating rival systems should consider whether they invert the proper priority of subjectivity and objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indestructibility of the subjective/internal grounds permanence of the objective/external
rubrics_metrics.description: The permanence of the objective (species, phenomena) can only be the phenomenal appearance of the indestructibility of the subjective or internal; the root of things lies in that which they are for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging claims about what 'really is', prefer accounts that ground external permanence in an underlying enduring subjectivity (the will) rather than vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrinal consistency requires pre-birth existence for true immortality
rubrics_metrics.description: Brahmanism and Buddhism consistently hold both continued existence after death and existence before birth, on the ground that the soul would not be eternal if it were a production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate doctrines of immortality for internal consistency: if immortality is asserted, consider whether a doctrine coherently accounts for both pre-birth and post-death existence to avoid the paradox of a production leading to eternity.
